title: Electrons and Photons — MCQs
description: NEB Grade XII Physics - Interactive MCQ Presentation

questions.q: Who performed the oil drop experiment?
questions.explanation: Robert Millikan conducted the famous oil drop experiment from 1906-1913. This experiment measured the charge of an individual electron and provided evidence for the quantization of electric charge.

questions.q: What was the primary objective of Millikan's oil drop experiment?
options: To measure the charge of an electron and demonstrate charge quantization
To discover the existence of electrons
To measure the mass of oil drops
To study the viscosity of air
questions.explanation: The main goal was to determine the charge of a single electron by observing the motion of charged oil drops between parallel plates. This proved that electric charge is quantized in multiples of the electron charge (e).

questions.q: In Millikan's experiment, what condition exists when the oil drop is stationary?
options: Electric force equals gravitational force (qE = mg)
Electric force is greater than gravitational force
Gravitational force is greater than electric force
No forces act on the drop
questions.explanation: When the electric force balances the gravitational force, the oil drop remains stationary. Mathematically: qE = mg, where q is charge, E is electric field, m is mass, and g is gravitational acceleration.

questions.q: How does Millikan's experiment suggest quantization of charge?
options: Charge on drops are always integer multiples of a fundamental unit (electron charge)
questions.explanation: Millikan observed that the charge on different oil drops was always a whole number multiple of a smallest charge unit (~1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C). This proved that charge is quantized: Q = ne, where n is an integer and e is the elementary charge.

questions.q: What was used to create the electric field in Millikan's experiment?
options: Parallel metal plates with applied voltage
questions.explanation: A uniform electric field was created between two parallel horizontal plates. By adjusting the voltage, the electric field strength could be controlled to balance the weight of oil drops.

questions.q: In Millikan's experiment, an oil drop of mass 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg is suspended between plates. If E = 2 × 10⁵ N/C, what is the charge on the drop? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: At equilibrium: qE = mg. So q = mg/E = (2.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 10)/(2 × 10⁵) = (2.0 × 10⁻¹⁴)/(2 × 10⁵) = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, which equals one elementary charge (1e).

questions.q: What does the observation that all charges are multiples of 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C prove?
options: Charge is quantized and this value is the elementary charge
All masses are related to this value
All particles have the same charge
questions.explanation: This observation proved that electric charge cannot take any arbitrary value but exists only in multiples of a fundamental unit called the elementary charge (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C), providing direct evidence for charge quantization.

questions.q: If Millikan measured charges of -3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, -6.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and -8.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ C on different drops, what is the elementary charge?
questions.explanation: The charges are: -2e, -4e, and -5e respectively. The greatest common divisor is e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. This represents the elementary charge carried by a single electron.

questions.q: How does an electron move when placed in a uniform electric field?
options: It accelerates in the direction opposite to the field
It accelerates in the direction of the field
It moves in a circular path
questions.explanation: Since electrons are negatively charged, the electric force on them is F = -eE, which is opposite to the field direction. The electron accelerates opposite to the electric field with acceleration a = eE/m.

questions.q: What is the force on an electron in an electric field E?
questions.explanation: The force on an electron is F = qE where q = -e (negative charge). Therefore F = -eE, meaning the force is opposite to the electric field direction. The magnitude is F = eE.

questions.q: Derive the acceleration of an electron in a uniform electric field.
questions.explanation: Using Newton's second law: F = ma. Since F = eE (magnitude), we get eE = ma, so a = eE/m. This shows acceleration is proportional to field strength and inversely proportional to electron mass.

questions.q: An electron enters a uniform electric field perpendicularly. What is its trajectory?
questions.explanation: When an electron enters perpendicular to a uniform electric field, it experiences constant acceleration in the field direction while maintaining constant velocity perpendicular to it, resulting in a parabolic trajectory similar to projectile motion.

questions.q: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference V. What is its final velocity?
questions.explanation: Using energy conservation: Work done = Change in KE. eV = ½mv². Solving for v: v = √(2eV/m). This is the velocity gained by an electron accelerated through potential V.

questions.q: What force acts on an electron moving in a magnetic field?
options: Lorentz force: F = evB sinθ (perpendicular to both v and B)
questions.explanation: The magnetic force on a moving charge is F = qvB sinθ. For an electron (q = e) moving perpendicular to field (θ = 90°), F = evB. This force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes direction but not speed.

questions.q: When an electron moves perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field, what is its path?
options: Circular path with radius r = mv/(eB)
questions.explanation: The magnetic force provides centripetal acceleration. evB = mv²/r, so r = mv/(eB). The electron moves in a circle with this radius. The period is T = 2πm/(eB), independent of velocity.

questions.q: Derive the radius of circular motion of an electron in a magnetic field.
questions.explanation: For circular motion in a magnetic field, magnetic force = centripetal force: evB = mv²/r. Solving for r: r = mv/(eB). This radius depends on electron momentum and inversely on magnetic field strength.

questions.q: What is the period of circular motion of an electron in a magnetic field?
questions.explanation: The period T = 2πr/v = 2π(mv/(eB))/v = 2πm/(eB). Remarkably, this is independent of velocity! This is called the cyclotron frequency and is fundamental to cyclotron operation.

questions.q: An electron enters a magnetic field of 0.5 T perpendicularly with velocity 2 × 10⁶ m/s. What is the radius of its circular path? (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
In a crossed electric and magnetic field, when does an electron move in a straight line?
options: When electric force equals magnetic force: eE = evB
questions.explanation: For straight-line motion, the net force must be zero. eE = evB, so v = E/B. This condition is used in velocity selectors in instruments like mass spectrometers to select particles with specific velocities.

questions.q: Who discovered the electron and in what year?
questions.explanation: J.J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 through his cathode ray tube experiments. He demonstrated that cathode rays consisted of negatively charged particles much smaller than atoms.

questions.q: What is a cathode ray?
options: A stream of electrons emitted from the cathode
questions.explanation: Cathode rays are streams of electrons produced when a high voltage is applied between a cathode and anode in a vacuum tube. These rays travel from the cathode (negative electrode) to the anode (positive electrode).

questions.q: In Thomson's cathode ray tube, what evidence showed that cathode rays are negatively charged?
options: They were deflected toward the positive electrode
They were deflected toward the negative electrode
questions.explanation: When an electric field was applied, cathode rays deflected toward the positive electrode (anode), proving they carried negative charge. This was the key evidence distinguishing them from light.

questions.q: What was the role of the magnetic field in Thomson's experiment?
options: To deflect cathode rays perpendicular to the electric field deflection
questions.explanation: Thomson used both electric and magnetic fields. The magnetic field deflected rays in a direction perpendicular to the electric deflection. By balancing both fields, he could determine the velocity of electrons.

questions.q: How did Thomson calculate the mass-to-charge ratio (m/e) of the electron?
options: By measuring deflections in electric and magnetic fields and using the equations of motion
questions.explanation: Thomson set up equations balancing the electric and magnetic forces. By measuring the deflections in each field separately, he could calculate both the velocity (v = E/B) and the ratio m/e using the deflection equations.

questions.q: In Thomson's method, when the electric and magnetic fields balance, what is true about the electron?
options: Electric force equals magnetic force: eE = evB, so v = E/B
questions.explanation: When balanced, the net force is zero, and the electron travels in a straight line. eE = evB gives v = E/B. This undeflected beam allows calculation of electron velocity without knowing e or m separately.

questions.q: What was the significance of Thomson's determination of m/e ratio?
options: It showed electrons were fundamental particles with properties different from atoms
It measured the size of atoms
It determined the speed of light
questions.explanation: Thomson's m/e ratio (approximately 1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg) showed that electrons were much lighter than atoms and had a much larger charge-to-mass ratio. This led to the conclusion that electrons were fundamental particles.

questions.q: What is the magnitude of the charge on an electron?
questions.explanation: The elementary charge e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. This is the charge magnitude on an electron. All charges in nature are whole number multiples of this fundamental unit.

questions.q: What is the rest mass of an electron?
questions.explanation: The electron rest mass m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg or about 0.511 MeV/c². This is approximately 1/1836 of the proton mass, making the electron the lightest known fundamental particle.

questions.q: What is the charge-to-mass ratio (e/m) of an electron?
questions.explanation: e/m = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg. This ratio was one of the first fundamental constants measured and was crucial in early atomic physics.

questions.q: In a cathode ray tube (CRT), what accelerates electrons from cathode to anode?
options: High accelerating voltage between cathode and anode
questions.explanation: A high voltage (typically kV) is applied between the cathode and anode, creating a strong electric field that accelerates electrons. This gives them kinetic energy proportional to the voltage: KE = eV.

questions.q: How do the deflection plates in a CRT function?
options: They apply electric fields perpendicular to the electron beam to deflect it
They accelerate electrons along the tube axis
questions.explanation: Deflection plates create electric fields perpendicular to the electron beam. By varying the voltage on these plates, the beam can be scanned across the screen, which is the principle of CRT displays.

questions.q: What is the principle of a mass spectrometer?
options: Using electric and magnetic fields to separate particles by their mass-to-charge ratio
questions.explanation: A mass spectrometer uses a velocity selector (crossed fields) followed by a magnetic field region where particles with different m/q ratios follow different circular paths, allowing separation and analysis of isotopes and particles.

questions.q: What was Thomson's model of the atom?
options: A sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it (plum pudding model)
questions.explanation: Thomson proposed that atoms were spheres of positive charge with electrons distributed throughout, like plums in a pudding. This model was later replaced by Rutherford's nuclear model based on alpha particle scattering experiments.

questions.q: How are electron beams generated in cathode ray tubes?
options: By thermionic emission from a heated cathode
questions.explanation: Thermionic emission occurs when a heated cathode (filament) releases electrons due to thermal energy overcoming the work function. These electrons are then accelerated and focused to form a beam.

questions.q: Why does an electron moving in a magnetic field not gain or lose energy?
options: Because magnetic force is always perpendicular to velocity (does no work)
Because electrons don't interact with magnetic fields
Because electrons move at constant speed
questions.explanation: The magnetic force F = q(v × B) is always perpendicular to the velocity vector. Since Work = F·d and F ⊥ d, the work done is zero, so kinetic energy (and speed) remain constant.

questions.q: What was the key experimental setup that allowed Thomson to determine electron velocity?
options: Crossed electric and magnetic fields where undeflected rays pass when eE = evB
questions.explanation: By using crossed (perpendicular) electric and magnetic fields, Thomson created a velocity selector. Only electrons with v = E/B pass undeflected. This allowed precise velocity measurement without knowing e or m individually.

questions.q: An electron travels horizontally between parallel plates with electric field E pointing downward. What is its trajectory?
options: Parabolic path curving upward (opposite to field)
questions.explanation: The electron (negative charge) experiences an upward force opposite to the downward field. It maintains constant horizontal velocity while accelerating upward, creating a parabolic trajectory like projectile motion.

questions.q: If an electron moves at an angle θ to a magnetic field, what is the component of force acting on it?
questions.explanation: The magnetic force is F = q(v × B), giving magnitude F = evB sin(θ). Only the velocity component perpendicular to B (v sin θ) contributes. The parallel component (v cos θ) is unaffected.

questions.q: Why does Millikan's experiment specifically use oil drops rather than water droplets?
options: Oil drops evaporate slowly, allowing long observation periods
questions.explanation: Oil has very low evaporation rate, allowing observations to last hours without significant change in drop mass. Water evaporates quickly, making measurements unreliable.

questions.q: What is the approximate size of an electron according to classical physics?
questions.explanation: The classical electron radius (re = 2.8 × 10⁻¹⁵ m) is derived from equating electron's rest mass energy to electrostatic energy. However, quantum mechanics shows electrons don't have a well-defined size.

questions.q: What equation was used by Thomson to find m/e from deflection measurements?
options: From electric deflection: y = eEL²/(2mv₀²) where L is plate length and y is deflection
questions.explanation: For an electron entering horizontally between parallel plates, the vertical deflection is y = eEL²/(2mv₀²). By measuring y, E, L, and v₀ (from the balanced field condition), m/e can be calculated.

questions.q: What is the cyclotron frequency of an electron in a magnetic field?
questions.explanation: The cyclotron frequency (or Larmor frequency) is f = eB/(2πm). This is the frequency at which electrons orbit in a magnetic field, independent of their speed or radius of orbit.

questions.q: In Millikan's experiment, if a drop has charge -3e, what relationship exists between electric force and weight?
options: Electric force can be exactly 3 times the weight at suitable field strength
Electric force is always less than weight
Electric force is always greater than weight
questions.explanation: For a drop with charge q = -3e in upward field E: F = 3eE upward. Weight = mg downward. At equilibrium: 3eE = mg. By adjusting E, any relationship can be achieved, allowing measurement of integer multiples of e.

questions.q: An electron is deflected through 1 cm while traveling 5 cm horizontally between parallel plates. If plate separation is 2 cm and voltage is 1000 V, what is the electron's initial velocity?
What historical significance did the discovery of the electron have?
options: It proved atoms are divisible into smaller constituents, revolutionizing atomic theory
It determined the speed of light
questions.explanation: The discovery of the electron was revolutionary because it showed atoms contain smaller, fundamental particles. This led to the development of atomic models and quantum mechanics, fundamentally changing physics.

questions.q: In crossed fields with E perpendicular to B, what happens to an electron with v = E/B?
options: It travels in a straight line (velocity selector principle)
questions.explanation: When v = E/B, the electric and magnetic forces balance exactly: eE = evB. The net force is zero, so the electron travels undeflected in a straight line. This is the principle of a velocity selector.

questions.q: What observation led Thomson to conclude cathode rays were particles and not light?
options: They were deflected by both electric and magnetic fields
questions.explanation: Light is not deflected by electric or magnetic fields. Thomson showed that cathode rays were deflected in both fields, with the deflections consistent with negatively charged particles, proving they were material particles, not light.

questions.q: What determines the charge-to-mass ratio of an electron?
options: The magnitude of charge e and rest mass m are fundamental constants
questions.explanation: e and m are intrinsic properties of electrons—fundamental constants of nature. The ratio e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg is characteristic of electrons and doesn't change under normal circumstances.

questions.q: Why is the cyclotron frequency independent of an electron's speed?
options: T = 2πm/(eB) depends only on m, e, and B; not on v
Electrons always move at the same speed
Magnetic field only acts on slow electrons
The radius doesn't change with speed
questions.explanation: The period T = 2πm/(eB) is derived from T = 2πr/v where r = mv/(eB). The v cancels out, giving T independent of speed. This remarkable property is used in cyclotrons.

questions.q: How did the work of Millikan and Thomson complement each other?
options: Thomson measured m/e ratio; Millikan measured e separately, allowing calculation of m
questions.explanation: Thomson (1897) found e/m ≈ 1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg. Millikan (1906-1913) determined e ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C through the oil drop experiment. This allowed the electron mass to be calculated: m = e/(e/m) = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
